claims.text: The initial sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution.
Heating sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles from room temperature to 1000 K in vacuum triggers rapid phase separation.
Heating triggers surface-energy-driven segregation in these nanoparticles.
The phase separation and segregation override the hypothesized sluggish-diffusion stabilization.
The loss of the smallest particles is driven by Ostwald ripening.
Particle shape changes are driven by surface-energy minimization.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy constituents and preferentially segregate to particle surfaces.
Elevated temperature enhances diffusion sufficiently to permit rapid structural evolution.
Surface diffusion pathways dominate the structural evolution of sub-10 nm particles.
The high surface-to-volume ratio causes kinetic surface effects to dominate over configurational-entropy stabilization.
Chemical-potential gradients between differently sized particles cause smaller particles to dissolve and material to redeposit on larger particles.
Heating produces Au/Cu-rich surface layers and Co/Ni/Pt-rich cores.
The smallest particles disappear through dissolution and redeposition on larger particles.
Initially spherical particles evolve into faceted or irregular morphologies.
Sluggish diffusion has previously been reported as a characteristic of high-entropy alloys.
Under the sluggish-diffusion assumption, these nanoparticles should retain a single phase, particle size, and shape up to 1000 K.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption holds only above 50 nm or in bulk alloys and breaks down below 10 nm.
Vacuum prevents oxidation during heating.
The proposed surface-driven behavior should become observable within minutes above 600 K.
The exact transition temperature and the effects of specific elemental interactions on segregation kinetics are uncertain.
